cases.query: Find "Attention Is All You Need" and explain self-attention in the Transformer architecture.
cases.review_focus: The original proposes an attention-based architecture without recurrent or convolutional sequence modelling; related-paper summaries must not be mistaken for the original.
cases.overview: The Transformer architecture introduced in "Attention Is All You Need" (S1) replaces recurrent and convolutional components with multi‑head self‑attention and positional encodings, enabling parallel processing and achieving state‑of‑the‑art results on machine translation. Subsequent work has applied self‑attention to a variety of domains: video classification using space‑time attention (S8), blind room‑volume estimation in audio (S3), long‑time quantum dynamics prediction (S6), and retrieval tasks where performance depends entirely on self‑attention layers (S2). Recent studies also explore efficiency‑focused variants such as linear attention and state‑space models (S5), recurrent‑augmented heads (S7), and methods for interpreting attention maps (S12, S13).

findings.text: Self‑attention alone enables high‑quality machine translation, outperforming recurrent and convolutional baselines (S1).

findings.text: Sparsifying self‑attention to 15% of heads retains near‑perfect retrieval while preserving 84% MMLU performance (S2).
sources: Some Attention is All You Need for Retrieval

findings.text: Linear attention and state‑space models achieve reduced computational complexity compared to full self‑attention (S5).

citation_status.root_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

cases.overview: Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) is a paradigm that combines an external retrieval module with a language‑model generator to produce grounded text.  The 2020 study (S1) observes that large pre‑trained language models store factual knowledge in their parameters but still lag behind task‑specific architectures on knowledge‑intensive tasks, and it identifies the provision of provenance and the ability to update world knowledge as open research problems.  Subsequent work has explored different retrieval strategies and application domains.  The 2024 EVOR pipeline (S4) introduces a synchronous evolution of queries and diverse knowledge bases to adapt to domain‑specific knowledge, while the 2022 Multi‑Task RAG study (S5) demonstrates that relevance sampling can clean training data and enable a single Fusion‑in‑Decoder (FiD) generator to perform well across multiple knowledge‑intensive tasks.  These studies collectively illustrate the flexibility of RAG and highlight remaining challenges such as retrieval latency, dynamic knowledge base management, and robustness to adversarial retrieval attacks.

findings.text: Large pre‑trained language models store factual knowledge but still lag behind task‑specific architectures on knowledge‑intensive tasks, and providing provenance remains an open problem.

findings.text: Dynamic, context‑aware retrieval that evolves queries and knowledge bases during generation can adapt to domain‑specific knowledge, as demonstrated by the EVOR pipeline.

findings.text: Relevance sampling can clean training data and enable a single Fusion‑in‑Decoder generator to perform well across multiple knowledge‑intensive tasks.

citation_status.root_title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

cases.overview: LoRA (Low‑Rank Adaptation) is a parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning technique that freezes the pre‑trained weights of a large language model and injects trainable low‑rank matrices into selected layers, dramatically reducing the number of trainable parameters while preserving strong downstream performance (S1). Subsequent work has built on this core idea to address remaining gaps: Task‑Relevant Feature Enhancement augments LoRA with additional modules to capture task‑specific signals (S2); Dynamic Tangent‑Space LoRA expands the update space beyond the static tangent of the low‑rank factors (S3); Bias‑Alleviating LoRA introduces components to mitigate the propagation of pre‑training biases (S4); SPIRA proposes sparse, structured rank adaptations for more targeted updates (S9); and DPAC presents a tri‑dimensional framework that decomposes weight updates into magnitude and direction components to improve parameter efficiency (S10).

findings.text: LoRA trains only the added low‑rank matrices (A and B) while freezing all pre‑trained weights (S1).

findings.text: Dynamic Tangent‑Space LoRA shows that residual gradient components outside the low‑rank tangent space contain most gradient energy, indicating a performance gap with full fine‑tuning (S3).

findings.text: Bias‑Alleviating LoRA identifies catastrophic inheritance as a risk of standard LoRA, motivating bias‑mitigation modules (S4).

findings.text: SPIRA replaces dense low‑rank updates with sparse, structured adaptations, targeting task‑salient regions (S9).

findings.text: DPAC proposes a tri‑dimensional framework that decomposes weight updates into magnitude and direction components to improve parameter efficiency (S10).

cases.query: Find "Graph Attention Networks" and explain neighbourhood attention.
cases.review_focus: Neighbour weighting through attention should be grounded in the retrieved GAT paper.
cases.overview: Graph Attention Networks (GATs) introduced by Veliček et al. (2017) propose masked self‑attentional layers that let each node compute a weighted combination of its immediate neighbours' features, learning edge‑specific attention coefficients without requiring costly spectral matrix operations (S1). Subsequent extensions have adapted the core attention mechanism to new settings: Signed Graph Attention Networks incorporate sign‑aware aggregation for positive and negative edges (S2); DeepGAT addresses over‑smoothing in deep GAT stacks by proposing a layer‑wise depth‑adaptive scheme (S3); Spiking GATs replace dense softmax attention with spike‑based gating to reduce computation (S11); and Simplicial Attention Networks generalize attention to higher‑order simplicial complexes, attending over nodes, edges, and triangles (S13). These works collectively demonstrate the flexibility of neighbourhood‑centric attention across diverse graph modalities and application domains.

findings.text: GATs learn edge‑specific attention coefficients via masked self‑attention, enabling adaptive weighting of 1‑hop neighbours without spectral matrix operations (S1).
sources: Graph Attention Networks

findings.text: Signed Graph Attention Networks extend the GAT formulation to handle positive and negative edges, improving performance on signed network tasks (S2).
sources: Signed Graph Attention Networks

findings.text: DeepGAT introduces a depth‑adaptive mechanism to mitigate over‑smoothing in deep GAT stacks, allowing effective training of many attention layers (S3).
sources: Deep Graph Attention Networks

findings.text: Spiking GATs replace dense softmax attention with spike‑based gating, achieving lower computational cost while preserving attention dynamics (S11).
sources: Spiking GATs: Learning Graph Attentions via Spiking Neural Network

findings.text: Simplicial Attention Networks generalize attention to nodes, edges, and higher‑order simplices, demonstrating the versatility of masked self‑attention beyond standard graphs (S13).
sources: Simplicial Attention Neural Networks

cases.overview: Graph‑based approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) research has focused on constructing navigable proximity graphs that enable efficient greedy routing. 2016’s HNSW paper introduced a multi‑layer hierarchical NSW structure that eliminates the need for separate coarse search stages, while 2016’s EFANNA leveraged a kNN graph to accelerate search. 2024’s study on navigable graphs formalizes the notion of navigability and explores construction limits, and 2026’s I/O‑optimizations examine practical bottlenecks of disk‑resident ANN indices. 2025’s HENN proposes a hierarchical ε‑net navigation graph that aims to provide theoretical guarantees for graph‑based ANN methods.

cases.query: Find "Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation" and explain the error-correction setting.
cases.expected_title: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
cases.review_focus: Distinguish theoretical error-correction requirements from a claim of deployed fault-tolerant quantum computing.

citation_status.root_title: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation

cases.overview: Surface codes are a prominent family of quantum error‑correcting codes that encode logical qubits in a two‑dimensional array of physical qubits using stabilizer measurements. The 2012 article (S1) introduces the stabilizer formalism for surface codes, describes how logical qubits are formed from boundary defects, and provides numerical estimates of the resources required for fault‑tolerant operation, emphasizing compatibility with nearest‑neighbor hardware. Subsequent works explore complementary approaches: continuous‑time quantum error correction (CTQEC) that uses weak measurements and feedback (S3), error‑suppression techniques for adiabatic quantum computation (S6), and experimental demonstrations of surface‑code logical qubits with logical error per round below 1 % for distance‑3 and distance‑5 codes on a superconducting processor (S14). Additional studies address decoding and performance estimation, including a Markov‑chain Monte Carlo splitting method for rare‑event logical error rate estimation (S10) and analyses of distributed fault‑tolerant architectures (S11).

findings.text: Surface codes encode logical qubits in a 2‑D stabilizer lattice and provide numerical estimates of fault‑tolerance and resource requirements for large‑scale quantum computers (S1).
sources: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation

findings.text: Continuous‑time quantum error correction protects quantum information via weak measurements and real‑time feedback, offering an alternative to discrete syndrome extraction (S3).
sources: Continuous-time quantum error correction

findings.text: Adiabatic quantum computation can employ energy‑gap protection and dynamical decoupling to suppress errors, representing a distinct error‑handling paradigm from circuit‑model codes (S6).
sources: Error suppression and error correction in adiabatic quantum computation I: techniques and challenges

findings.text: Markov‑chain Monte Carlo splitting methods enable estimation of logical error rates deep in the rare‑event regime, though proposal trapping can affect sampling efficiency (S10).
sources: Fast and accurate rare-event simulation by Markov chain Monte Carlo for general quantum codes

findings.text: Experimental surface‑code implementations on a 120‑qubit superconducting processor achieve logical error per round below 1 % for distance‑3 and distance‑5 codes (S14).
sources: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
